# Linear Regression

::::: {.panel-tabset}

## Overview

Linear regression is a powerful analytical tool because it is easy to interpret while kept simple. Even so we can expand on it somewhat while still keeping it intelligable (Adding "switches" to make it two or more lines is a great example of an intelligable but more complex linear regression model)

## Mathematical Model

Here is the simple linear regression model:

$$
\underbrace{Y_i}_\text{Response} = \overbrace{\beta_0}^\text{y-int} + \overbrace{\beta_1}^\text{slope} \underbrace{X_i}_\text{Explanitory} + \overbrace{\epsilon_i}^\text{Error} \quad \text{where} \ \epsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)
$$

When we create a model ourselves it takes the form of:

$$
  \underbrace{\hat{Y}_i}_\text{Response} = \overbrace{b_0}^\text{est. y-int} + \overbrace{b_1}^\text{est. slope} \underbrace{X_i}_\text{Explanitory}
$$

Here we have the following interpretations ready made for us:
$\beta_0$ or Y intercept: This is the predicted value of the response variable when the explanitory variable is 0. This can be useful when $x=0$ has meaning
- For example: say we were predicting salary based on years of experience. The $\beta_0$ would be the salary expected when the applicant had 0 years of experience

$\beta_1$ or the slope: this is the change per unit. So for our earlier example this would be the increase in salary per year of experience

We can keep these interpretaions when looking at a **two lines model** as follows:

$$
\underbrace{Y_{i}}_\text{Response} = \overbrace{\beta_0}^\text{y-int} + \overbrace{\beta_1}^\text{slope} \underbrace{X_{1i}}_\text{Explanitory1} + \overbrace{\beta_2}^\text{Change y-int}\underbrace{X_{2i}}_\text{Explanitory2} + \overbrace{\beta_3}^\text{Change in slope} \underbrace{{X_{1i}}:{X_{2i}}}_\text{Interaction} + \overbrace{\epsilon_i}^\text{Error} \quad \text{where} \ \epsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)
$$

When we create a model ourselves it takes the form of:

$$
  \underbrace{\hat{Y}_{i}}_\text{Response} = \overbrace{\beta_0}^\text{y-int} + \overbrace{\beta_1}^\text{slope} {X_{1i}} + \overbrace{\beta_2}^\text{Change y-int}{X_{2i}} + \overbrace{\beta_3}^\text{Change in slope} \underbrace{{X_{1i}}:{X_{2i}}}_\text{Interaction} 
$$

Here we must now add two interpretations:

$\beta_2$ or Change in Y intercept: This functions only when $X_{2i}\neq0$ and disapeares when this "switch" is turned off. If we consider the earlier example and say the $X_{2i}$ is a binary variable whether or not the applicant has a college degree than this would be the change in the 0 years experience salary when the applicant also has a college degree. If he does not then the variable becomes 0 and the whole second half of the model would go away leaving only the simple linear regression from earlier.

$\beta_3$ or change in slope: is very similar to $\beta_2$ except with the slope in mind instead. If this is a positive number then the college degree holding applicants gain more per year experience then the non degree holders. 

**PLEASE NOTE** That $\beta_2$ and $\beta_3$ must be interpreted together with their baseline $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$
